title: Pinch pot ring dish set of three
subtitle: Three small matching pinch-pot ring dishes in air-dry clay, graduated sizes
excerpt: A ring dish set is three small open bowls in air-dry clay, made by the pinch pot method: a ball of clay opened and thinned by pressing the thumb and fingers together. The three dishes graduate in size from 6 cm to 10 cm across, designed to hold rings, earrings, and small everyday jewellery. No kiln is needed. Beginner makers new to pinch work can complete all three pieces in a single session with consistent results.
sourceNotes: Pinch pot method derived from first principles. The pinch pot is among the oldest hand-building techniques in ceramics, appearing in pottery traditions worldwide from the Neolithic period onward.

glossaryTerms.definition: A hand-building method in which a ball of clay is opened by the thumb and shaped by pinching the walls between thumb and fingers
The drying stage at which clay holds its shape firmly but is still cool to the touch and can be refined
Fully air-dried clay that is pale, lightweight, and ready to paint and seal

content.text: A ring dish set is three small open bowls in air-dry clay, shaped by the
pinch pot

method and graduated from about 6 cm to 10 cm across. They are designed to hold rings, earrings, and small jewellery on a dressing table or bedside. No kiln is needed. A beginner making their first pinch pots will find three dishes in one session gives enough repetition to improve markedly from the first dish to the third.

materials.name: Air-dry clay
materials.quantity: 300 g total (roughly 50 g, 90 g, and 160 g per dish)

materials.name: Matte acrylic varnish or PVA diluted 50/50 (for sealing)

content.text: Preparation

Weigh the clay before starting: 50 g for the small dish, 90 g for the medium, and 160 g for the large. Roll each portion into a smooth ball with no air pockets or cracks on the surface. Press any surface cracks closed by rolling the ball firmly between both palms before starting to pinch. Work from largest to smallest: the large dish teaches you the rhythm; the smaller dishes reward the control you build.
Making each dish
The method is the same for all three dishes. Repeat it for each ball of clay.

Hold the clay ball in one cupped hand. Press your other thumb into the centre of the ball, stopping about 5 mm from the bottom. The base of the dish should be 5-6 mm thick; going through creates a hole that is hard to fix.

Pinch the wall between your thumb inside the pot and your first two fingers outside, pressing gently and rotating the ball a small step after each pinch. Work in a spiral from the base upward, keeping the pinches close together (about 5 mm apart). The wall will begin to thin and widen.

Keep the wall thickness as even as possible: aim for 5-6 mm throughout. Thin patches will dry faster than thick areas and may crack. If you feel a thin area, stop pinching there and move to a thicker section, gradually evening out the wall.

Continue pinching and rotating until the dish has opened to the target diameter: roughly 6 cm for the small, 8 cm for the medium, and 10 cm for the large. The rim should be roughly level. If the rim becomes wavy and uneven, that is normal: it will be refined at leather-hard.

Set the dish on a flat surface and press the base gently down to flatten it. The base must be flat enough that the dish does not rock. If the base is too rounded, press it against the table top very gently to flatten a small area without pushing through the clay.
Use a damp wooden rib to smooth the interior of the dish, working in circular strokes from the base upward. The rib removes fingerprints and evens out pinch marks.
Leave each dish to reach leather-hard (firm but still cool and slightly flexible) over 2-4 hours before refining the rim. The rim is easier to trim cleanly when the clay has stiffened a little.
At
leather-hard

, trim the rim level with the needle tool, cutting away any uneven high points. Smooth the cut rim with a damp sponge, running the sponge in a single direction around the rim to leave a clean edge without dragging the clay.

Make three small open bowls using the pinch pot method. Graduate them in size: 6 cm, 8 cm, and 10 cm across. They hold rings and earrings on a dressing table. No kiln is needed. Three dishes in one session gives you enough practice to improve as you go.
Drying
Allow each dish to dry uncovered from
leather-hard
to
bone-dry

at room temperature. Small dishes dry in one to two days; the large in two to three days. Do not place near a heat source to speed drying: uneven heat creates cracks at the thinner wall sections. A bone-dry dish is pale, lightweight, and no longer cool to the touch.
Finishing

Paint the bone-dry dishes before sealing. A white base coat followed by one colour gives a clean, unified look across the set. Seal with two coats of diluted PVA or matte varnish, inside and out. Stick a small felt pad to the base of each dish to protect furniture surfaces.
Care

These dishes are decorative. Do not use them for food or drink. Air-dry clay is not waterproof even when sealed: wipe the interior with a dry cloth only. Do not put in a dishwasher or submerge in water. Handle with care, as thin pinched rims are the most fragile part of the piece.
Variations

Press a simple botanical impression into the interior base of each dish before the clay stiffens. Use a single small leaf pressed into the centre, then remove it carefully. The impression becomes a feature when the dish is used for jewellery and the base is visible.

Add a small rolled clay peg inside the large dish to hold rings upright. Press a short clay cylinder (about 1.5 cm tall and 1 cm wide) into the centre of the base with slip at leather-hard. Allow to dry separately before sealing, then bond with PVA once the base coat is applied.

Pinch the rim of all three dishes into a gentle petal shape by pressing evenly spaced indentations around the rim at leather-hard using a fingertip and thumb: five indentations on the small dish, six on the medium, eight on the large. This gives the set a delicate fluted edge.
Troubleshooter

items.problem: A hole appears in the base during pinching
items.cause: The thumb was pushed too far down through the clay, or the base area was pinched instead of only the walls
items.fix: Patch the hole immediately with a small piece of fresh clay, pressing it firmly and blending with a damp finger on both sides. If the hole is large, roll the clay back into a ball and start again

items.problem: Walls crack at the rim during drying
items.cause: The rim was pinched thinner than the wall below it, causing faster drying and shrinkage cracking at the thinnest point
items.fix: At leather-hard, dampen the crack with a wet finger and press closed. Blend with a wooden rib. Keep the dish loosely covered for a further 12 hours to slow drying at the rim

items.problem: The three dishes look very different in shape
items.cause: Pinch force was inconsistent between pieces, leading to varying wall slopes and rim heights
items.fix: At leather-hard, compare the three dishes and gently press any that are taller inward at the walls to lower the rim height. Accept some natural variation: hand-built pieces are not supposed to be identical

items.problem: Base rocks when placed on a flat surface
items.cause: The base was not flattened enough during forming, leaving a rounded base instead of a flat foot
items.fix: At leather-hard, press the base onto a flat tile or board and hold firmly for a few seconds. If already bone-dry, glue a small cork pad to the lowest point of the curved base to stabilise it
